called due to battery not charging although we spent the money to hard wire it..... and got an email from them. box says it works to -5F. this is what the email states..... Important temperatures

The following are key temperatures to watch out for in regards to your batteries.

36°F (3°C): The battery may not hold a charge as effectively, resulting in you having to charge the unit more frequently.
32°F (0°C): The battery may not charge at all. Even hardwired configurations may not charge the battery.
-5°F (-20.5°C): The battery may stop working completely until temperatures warm up.
What to do when it gets cold

Bring your device inside: When it gets cold and your device's battery runs out, bring your entire device inside and charge the battery with a USB cord. This will allow your device to warm up while the battery charges.
Make sure your battery is charged to 100%: When charging your battery, be sure that it reaches 100% before your remount the device. While the battery still won't be as effective as when the temperatures are warmer, making sure that the battery is at 100% will allow your device to work as long as possible.
Monitor your charge and the temperature: As long as the temperature hovers around the points listed above, you may have issues with battery charge. Therefore it's important to constantly monitor your battery life when it gets cold to make sure your device is always working.

Living in Houston, I have owned several weather radios in this price range over the years. This radio is my favorite.

I like the fact that you can re-charge it easily with AAA batteries (not included). I have found that re-charging with a hand-crank is too slow. Solar re-charging works well on most devices if you keep the device stored on a windowsill for the year so that it is fully charged during a weather event. Having the option to use three AAA batteries is great because the radio can be ready to use immediately. Another feature that I like is that no screwdriver is needed in order to open the compartment in order to change-out the batteries. This is important when evacuating and also when the power goes out.

During Hurricane Ike, I evacuated to a friend's home. The storm made landfall around midnight or so. In the dark, it is hard to find anything, so it's good to be ready before the lights go out. I can remember lying in bed alone listening to my friend's radio (not this radio) in the dark as the NOAA forecaster reported the progress of the surge up through Galveston Bay and into the bayous, lakes, and streams inland. It was so helpful to know exactly what was happening to the area in which I lived.

My friend's radio was a very expensive radio, and the main difference between her radio and this radio seems to be the reception.

Hers ran all night with no interruption with reception. With this radio, I do have to turn the radio off and then back on if I lose reception to the channel. A really expensive weather radio would probably have better reception if you want to listen non-stop.

For my needs, however, this radio is excellent and is the best that I have owned in its price range.

Cut the cord with cable 2 days ago but wanted local channel access. Streaming services are nice but you are forever going from one platform to another to channel surf which I find super frustrating. Good old tv with antenna is so much easier. This antenna took less than 5 minutes to set up. I put it up in the window. Channel scanned and was watching 43 channels like that! All crystal clear pictures. I must say that most towers are about 40 miles away from my home ,all kinda clustered together. They sit southeast of me and where I have the antenna sitting is close to southeasterly. Kind of a no brainer but I would suggest looking up tower locations  in your area. The map will display channels broadcast by this tower... and try to configure your antenna in that general direction. Makes sense to me. Very pleased with this antenna and purchase. Cut the cord with cable. You won't be disappointed :) UPDATE: This is an indoor antenna and they work best in a window and pointed towards the transmission towers in your area. You will get max channels that way. That's been my experience but I opted to use the double stick tape provided and mount mine outside taped to a beam on my metal pergola. Channel availability jumped up immediately upon rescanning so outdoor antennas are the way to go...and yes this is not truly recommended for outdoor use.. I went from 36 channels inside to 55 mounted outside the same window..3 months and I have had no issues with outside use. It hasn't fallen once..the weather has been all over the map..from sunny, rainy, and even the current blizzard conditions we have experienced...that includes rain, freezing rain, and snow. Maybe it will crap out over time but I paid 15 bucks for over 50channels. If it lasts a year thats only $1.25 a month to watch tv which is hella lot cheaper than cable. I'm super satisfied!!

Typically I stick to higher end gaming keyboards. Mechanical and optical switches are generally my go to. I had never used a keyboard from this brand before so when I was given the chance to grab one, I figured I would see how it stacks up.

So far I'm fairly impressed. I've used some tournament edition keyboards with the smaller form factor from other brands so I knew what I was getting into when it came to the size of the keyboard. All in all, sizing is fine. They key placement and distance between keys works fine. I do run into issues at times where my fingers get lost on the right side of the keyboard. Getting used to that will come in time though. The key response is quick. They are mechanical switches but they do manage to deaden the sound a bit which is nice. The RGB features are basic at best. You have a few settings you can select from and all of it is done directly on the keyboard itself. It has your normal basic modes. It illuminates well though and you can increase/decrease the brightness. The build quality is nice. For being a 75% keyboard, it has some weight to it. I like the fact the keys are labeled for both Mac and PC. I primarily use it on my PC though. The place where it seems to shine is in the connectivity department. I can connect it by bluetooth to numerous devices or I can have it wired. I generally run wired to my main PC and if I need to use it on my MacBook or other devices, I just unplug it from the PC and connect by BT to the other device. It works out nicely.

From a gaming standpoint (which I do a lot of), I'm not certain that I like it as much yet. Emphasis on the "yet". I know it takes some time to become accustomed to a new keyboard. The response and feel. I'm going to continue gaming on it for a while to see if I become more adapted to it. It just feels different than what I'm used to. It most likely has to do with the key spacing more so than anything else.

This is definitely a nice keyboard and I recommend it. I will most likely continue to use it as my daily keyboard for a while longer to see how it holds up over time.

As all computer professionals can attest dust collection can be a major issue for computers internal components. As the internal fans work to pull air in to cool the computer it also will pull in dust through every open port. While the air vents typically have screens that help collect this the ports do not - this is where plugs are so important.

I utilize port plugs on all of my devices - computers, switches, cameras, TVs, any port not in use has a plug to prevent both dust and moisture intrusion.

These plugs click into place and perform exactly as they should protecting your equipment.

This is an excellent set that is well worth the investment.

This is a neat circuit for experimenting/demonstrating induction heating, but the circuit is highly is highly fragile and prone to burning out the power mosfets if too much mass is being heated or if the metal isn't placed absolutely in the center of the coil. This is the second one that I burned out after using the first one for less than 24 hours. The moment it burns out, you'll see a small puff of white smoke come out near the toroidal inductor, the power LED will stills stay on, but will no longer heat up. Because of how delicate this is, there's really not much you can use it this circuit for other than heating up paperclips

I have a bathtub that obviously USED TO have strips of gravel coating to prevent slipping.  Well, the gravel coating had long since run out, so the tub was very slick.  I was shocked because I live in a Seniors Independent Living home - I submitted a "ticket" over a month ago and since they are way understaffed right now they couldn't get to me in a reasonable time - so I bought these to substitute for that grainly strips that used to be in the tub.  My installation isn''t perfect I can see a couple look a bit crooked but I didn't have the right kind of ruler to space them properly.  Thankfully I have a good eye for what is straight and what is crooked so overall I was able to space most of them 100% straight and at the same distance as the row before.  Got them on in about 20 minutes, let them set for a little over 48 hours - using a hospital "soap" to stay clean until I could take a shower (I barely sweat so that was more than sufficient).  Strangely I even enjoyed putting them on.  They look great, they stick 100% and are easily as good as the old gravel type strips I've used in other tubs.  So I give this product a 5.  If your eyesight is poor, use a ruler to keep these straight and evenly distant or just make your own decorative pattern in the tub floor.  As long as they cover the main part of where you shower you don't have to cover the entire floor of the tub.  Mine were just as long as the gravel strips that had been there before and worn off.  Time will tell how long they will last, but they are inexpensive and easy to reinstall (although I suspect getting them all up could be quite difficult.)

First of all, I am a Chef...I've worked in fine Restaurants all over the country...Started out in High School as the youngest Prep Chef/Sous Chef in Henris' History while a Senior in school and working part time in Chicago. I have owned (and still own) Henkel Knives, Custom jute and wax handle wrapped pans and even spatulas. I have owned many Cast Iron Pans and consider them to be the one of the most valued tool for any chef due to their sheer versatility and ease of use.

That said....I just lost my trusted old friend of 25 years....yeah my Cast Iron Skillet. I went to Amazon to find a WORTHY replacement. I found the Lodge Products and saw by the reviews, that this company was going to fit my needs perfectly.

How wrong I was!

I purchased the 10.5 inch cast iron skillet from Lodge. First notice after getting the skillet was the ROUGH, STIPPLED texture of the skillet. My other cast iron "champs" were SMOOTH like a teflon pan, and were easily SEASONED! This chunk of iron was rough and "pimpled" ...like I was as a teenager when I first worked as a line chef for Henrisis.!

Ok so I figured, "OK well, I'll just season the thing and all will be well in the Kitchen! NOT SO!

I started with my "tried-and-true" canola and sunflower oil @ 450f for an hour. OK. pan is still not seasoned. OK, do it again 4x and lets use GHEE (mp480f) this time. Still the surface looks my face when I was 13 years old....Yeah....full of bumps and no SMOOTH surface like with my last beloved cast iron wonder.

Conclusion, Yeah, these Lodge Folks do not know how to cast real fine cook ware. They need to figure out a way to create SMOOTH CASTED IRON COOKWARE. or just go away.

I will never buy another product from these PATZERS!

It would never go in a straight line, always went in a parabolic line, again missing many areas. Always seemed to be cleaning the same area. I put it on the Zig Zag pattern setting and it would still just go in random directions. I've brought in for service about a year or so after having it and the programing never improved. Still can't find its base and they are supposed to do a full cleaning and replacing of necessary parts but Bob still came back dirty. I stopped using it for a while. We moved to a house with all hardwood floors and thought this could be a chance for some redemtion but the same problems exist. All I can say is I'm very disappointed in Bob. I can see why people pay more money for the Roomba and other popular vacs instead. I would not recommend this to anyone.

While there are some good features for this cup and it does a pretty average job of insulating beverages, there are 2 negatives that make this a less than compelling purchase. For starters, the lid does not screw on and is neither secure nor leakproof. And while both a curved and straight metal straw set and cleaning tool accompany the cup, there is no dedicated insertion point for the straw. Instead, you must use it in the oval opening intended for sipping. The straw rattles around that opening and while it is possible to separately purchase silicone straw silencer sleeves, the larger problem is the fact that this opening substantially reduces the insulating effectiveness and results in your beverage losing either heat or cold far more quickly than a cup with a dedicated, tightly fitted straw opening. In fact, I purchased this cup as a replacement for a competitor’s model that eventually lost the gasket seal for its straw opening! Just that tiny round area being open to air dramatically reduced the overall effectiveness of its insulation and led to me purchasing this cup as a replacement. I did not expect the new cup to have an even larger open channel to the exterior! If you are looking for something that is truly well-insulated and seals tightly, you can pass this version by.

"Cons of Phenoxyethanol

The Dr prescribed terbafine, bit it had so many horrible side effects so I signed up for One Medical concierge Dr visit and went in. The second One Medical Dr said, that it looks like new nail growth, slightly thicker than my the old one growing out, and looked like remineralization, and asked me if I've been taking supplements, and I haven't. It perplexed us, but just to be sure, pictures were taken, prescribed antifungal nail polish to used for a month just to be sure, and a distilled vinegar foot bath for 15 min / daily and then every few days. Well, it only been a day and my toes nails looks amazing.

I had high hopes for learning about the positives of responsible drug use. As someone who belongs to a social group where responsible, adult drug use of mind-enhancing (low/non-addictive) drugs, I was excited to hear someone speak of this concept with scientific authority! Sadly, the author grossly and irresponsibly promotes highly addictive drugs and seems to pretend that there is no addictive quality. He overstates how big Pharma money and the government have downplayed the danger of these types of substances, especially opioids, instead of explaining the actual dangers. The worst part is that he uses himself and his own experiences as the control for most of his assumptions. Just because he has managed to take opioids including heroin without addiction (yet) does NOT mean that everyone will. And the consequences of being wrong about this assumption are catastrophic.

As the now ex wife of a man who was using opioids and other drugs “responsibly” for a while and who is now an addict whose life is falling apart, I can tell you firsthand that not everyone can do hard drugs responsibly. Hart gives a short disclaimer at the beginning about how the adults who try this should be mentally sound, careful people, which I agree with. But most people don’t know they’re not mentally sound until they find the means to start avoiding life on a destructive scale. He ignores the fact that almost everyone in this entire world has trauma. And that even for the small percentage who don’t, events could take place which would push their use from recreational to harmful. Furthermore, there is no discussion about the real dangers and actual effects of becoming an addict. He completely side steps the ACTUAL, REAL opioid epidemic as if it’s all propaganda and misinformation. I can personally witness that it is not! I kept waiting for him to address this angle on addiction and which substances were more dangerous and likely to be habit forming. But he repeatedly ignores it because HE doesn’t have a problem with it. For that reason I found this book incredibly dangerous and I am disappointed that he published it in the name of science.

The base for a British mini-series, and a more recent movie, this is probably the best of the John Le Carre British spy novels.  I was reminded of John Le Carre's books by his recent passing, he was an amazing writer even outside of spy genre, so I went back and am re-reading the George Smiley series.  This book is nothing at all like the Ian Fleming James Bond novels, no fancy cars or gadgets, the fights in the George Smiley universe are fought at an intellectual level, intertwined with uncertainty and very British levels of manners, conventions, and classes.  The protagonist does not really get the girl (at least in this novel), she factors in, but mostly he does not know where she is, and in fact has to puzzle that out as part of the plot.  As such, the protagonist is someone that you can relate to, a more normal person, someone his bosses and co-workers take advantage of, even his tailor sees him coming.  He is kind of down and out when the novel begins.  Thus the novel is about his struggle to come back, to get to the truth, which while kicked off by a lucky event or two, is that made more challenging both by where he begins, but also having to discover truths about his life and the Service that he would really rather not have learned .  His fight back is done intellectually.  We all might all aspire to be as smart as George Smiley, but few of us are.  And probably a lot of novelists aspire to write as well as John Le Carre, but very few are able to do it.  If you read only one George Smiley or John Le Carre novel, this is the one to read.

This is a rather odd book. The premise sounded interesting, but the execution left something to be desired. Solemn Redvine is a girl growing up in Mississippi. She lives in a trailer park that time forgot, which seems to lack basic running water, among other things. Her father is a notorious thief and philanderer, and possibly a murderer. Solemn thinks she saw him throw his mistress's baby down the trailer park's well. She makes friends with a neighbor, but then a lightning storm challenges that friendship. The baby's mother disappears and Solemn is determined to find her. To cope with it all, Solemn retreats into a world of dreams and fantasy, which are recounted in the book. I found they added little and were mostly a distraction. This is just the first half of the book. In the second half, Solemn goes with her father to rob a house and ends up getting all the blame (which her father is happy to let her take). She's then sent to a reformatory, and that's about it. This book had a winding, meandering, not well-connected plot. I was shocked to discover it was set in the late 20th century, as it reads like something more from the 40s or the 50s. In any case, while there were really compelling elements, this book was too all over the place to keep my attention.

(Review of Elvis Presley section only)
Bill O’Reilly took a very over-simplified look at the very complicated life of Elvis Presley. There are only 111 pages, with very large type, dedicated to 19 years of Presley’s life and those pages lack detail and are filled with inaccuracies (many are detailed in other reviews). This is a very lazily, internet-researched book. Peter Guralnick wrote over 600 pages to cover the same ground. ( I highy recommend)

There are a lot of statements made by O’Reilly with absolutely no support. He chose to take the sensational route. There are lots of opinions and implications that are not based in fact. Example – NO ONE tried to help Elvis with his drug addiction – FALSE.

Presley is portrayed as a country bumpkin who was too naïve to choose his own path and as the victim of everyone around him. In fact, Elvis was quite intelligent, but incredibly stubborn and made some very bad life choices with his eyes wide open. While there were unprecedented circumstances (never- before-seen levels of fame) surrounding Presley, the only person Elvis was a victim of was himself.

I chose not to read the Ali/Lennon sections because I am far less familiar with their stories and would be unable to discern fact from fiction.

I use these books when I was just starting out water coloring, and pulled them back out recently. Now that I have a couple of years of experience with it, I can say that, although they are a lot of fun, and definitely encourage you to work with watercolors, they also have some advice that will turn into bad habits and some challenges.

Two of the big challenges are, first, the paper is very heavily textured, more like hot press than cold press. This makes sharp lines and fine details quite difficult. It’s also prone to bleeding, which can make boundaries between colors hard to keep crisp. Second, the usual advice for watercolors is to start by painting light colors, and then move on to dark. This makes it a lot easier to control where your dark colors end up. The instructions for a lot of the images ignore this advice, and it does make it harder.

As other reviewers have noted, the colors for the sample images often don’t match the instructions, so if you want to make it, look like the pictures you off and have to be a little bit creative with your pallete. The sample images were, I think, painted larger and reduced for reproduction, which is fine, but getting the same level of fine detail on the small sketches is challenging, and could be frustrating if you don’t realize that’s what the difference is.

Despite all these problems, the books are fun, and they are a good way to practice water coloring on days that you don’t feel like being super creative but you still feel like getting some painting in. Just be aware that some of the instructions don’t instill the best habits.

I was sadly disappointed when I realized that this book is NOT about Sawbill as the title would lead you to believe. I read the parts about Sawbill in one sitting. The book is as the description says, ..."Case struggles to "live in place" without a geographical home". Perhaps a title more like 'Live in Place' or something less misleading would be nice. The book "Sawbill History and Tales" by Mary Alice Hansen is much more informative about Sawbill than this book. On page 203 of Case's book, she describes walking into Sawbill Outfitters store, sees 2 employees playing cribbage, assumes they know nothing about Sawbill Lodge without asking and leaves. I know there are several people on site that would have answered any questions she had about Sawbill Lodge. However, she was not referred to myself or anybody since she did not simply ask anyone at Sawbill? Many of the campers who are proud of how many decades their families have camped at Sawbill would have delighted in talking about the lodge. How could the college-aged employees that she assumes "are not from the area" know she wanted to talk about the lodge since she did not ask or identify herself? On page 202 she looks for the Lodge site without any help. The area she describes is not the Lodge site. She would have to go across the Sawbill Creek bridge beyond the mowed turnaround. There's a 6 foot tall rock foundation that was part of the old Lodge still standing. But I realize now this is NOT a book about Sawbill but somebody musing about places & her family. I think she was more there to be alone with her memories than research. If I had paid attention to the narrative about the book instead of the title, I would have thought twice about buying it. I am not native or a local at Sawbill but I've worked in the area since 1980. Chances are I was on site when she visited & left without saying anything. Side note: no way could I be mistaken for a college kid. ; ) I was standing in the crowd when they had the auction in 1983 with only $20 in my pocket. Got 2 wool blankets and a Dick Raiken table lamp. So bottom line:

This IS NOT a book about Sawbill.

The wonderful writing, combining beautiful prose, wit and gut-wrenching descriptive passages show her incredible courage and determination. Some of the close calls she experiences will make you shiver!

Women weren't working on the rails before her time. No one believed they could survive the conditions or even have the physical capability to do the job.

Her experience and her story, and that of the other female "rail boomers" she meets changed a lot of minds, including those of the hardest-core working men out there.

A great read for anyone who has a fascination, or even just a vague interest in the railroads.
The story of a whole other side, that I never read anywhere else.

P.S. You don't have to be a feminist to appreciate this book...

I love Bibles and inherited my grandmother's illustrated Bible when she passed away. The illustrations in her Bible are saturated with the deep colors and gravitas of Old Masters. There are approximately one or two in each book of the Bible.

I bought the Kregel's Treasury of Illustrated Bible Stories hoping it would be identical to my grandmother's Bible, but it has notable differences. It is not the same as hers at all, but I am buying one for each of my adults nieces and my nephew as well as one for myself.

Although some advertisements describe the Kregel Treasury as a children's Bible, the text is much too advanced for young children. Every page has a direct quote from a Biblical source and a facing illustration. The language and concepts are, in my opinion, suitable for young adults and adult readers.

Overall, however, the total impression is inspiring. While the colors are not as deep or rich as those in my grandmother's Bible, the illustrations are beautifully and respectfully presented. The different Biblical sources are interesting and accessible texts. What I like to do is just sit down and start reading randomly. I find that as I do so, I begin to journey through this book and shift my focus from the day's current events -- including the pandemic -- into a focused state of reading the Bible.

The more I read and use this book, the more I like it. It is a thoughtful gift that presents Biblical stories, parables, and lessons with pleasing illustrations by artists who have a history of creating Biblical illustrations for publication.

First of all, I write this review as a reformed Twihard. I was deep into the books 10-12 years ago (as an adult English professor, not an inexperienced preteen falling in love with fiction). Although the original books were - literarily speaking - nothing special, the characters and storyline captured my imagination. I read everything Stephenie Meyer wrote about Twilight, INCLUDING the first half of Midnight Sun that she had published on her website after someone had leaked it online. Eventually, I lost interest, grew less attached, and began to see how silly the books/movies were.

Fast forward to this summer when I saw this book appear on store shelves. I purchased it from Amazon out of curiosity. The beginning was very much how I remember the story that Meyer published online a few years ago. It was vaguely interesting because there was a bit that was different from Bella's side of the story. But then the book went on. And on. And on. Interminiably.

Spoilers ahead. (But are they really spoilers when this is the SAME book that we've all already read and watched a million times before??)

There was so much of the story that was just the same as the original Twilight story. At about halfway through the book, the two storylines merge so much that there's really nothing more to tell. The only thing that's different from Edward's perspective by the time they start to fall in love, is how much he loves her. And wants to kill her. And how he is such a creep (which has always been a common criticism of the Twilight books, but it's so much more apparent - and less forgivable - when you hear it from his perspective).

The famous meadow scene had to have been about 100 pages long.... about 85 pages longer than it needed to be.

The book wears on, making sure the reader understands in no uncertain terms how much Edward loves Bella, without revealing anything new about any character or any plot (with the possible exception of the very boring, very pointless wild goose-chase that Edward, Emmett, and Carlisle go on while Jasper, Alice, and Bella travel to Phoenix). Speaking of which, the only action (not to be confused with the introduction of the conflict) of the story, which we all know happens with the arrival of James, Victoria, and Laurant, doesn't happen until around pg. 500 and is wrapped up on page 583 of this 657-page paperweight.

I got the clear impression that S. Meyer finished this book under some sort of duress. Maybe her bank account needed it, or at some urging from her agent, but there was no heart in this book (not the part that was 'newly published' at any rate). The storytelling and the writing was lackluster, and as a matter of fact, the editor seemed to quit caring at some point in the last quarter because the flow of grammatical errors and typos just increased towards the end of the book. Maybe they figured no one would actually finish reading this book. Well, joke's on them because I rage-finished (if that's even a thing) this book. My misery is your gain; if you value your time or if want to leave the nostalgia of your innocent infatuation with Twilight in tact, do not read this book.

It is evident that the person who wrote this quick review sheet speaks Spanish in Spain and not in Central America. If you are learning Spanish Spanish, then that’s great. But if you are learning anything else, this is probably not going to be ultimately very useful for you.
That’s the thing that happens when you generalize an entire language. It’s strange, the word for shrimp on this sheet is gambas, but everyone else understands it to be camarones.
That’s just one difference, but I find several things on this worksheet to be not quite accurate. My advice, get a true Spanish mentor who understands language and grammar to explain to you the context. Context is all important. Rather than memorize words and phrases, try to find someone who teaches you real conversation. Words and phrases are helpful but will never get you into conversation. If you need help, visit abcspanishnow on I G. They have a better technique.

I keep trying Donna Leon’s Brunetti mysteries after swearing off them, in hopes the next one will show a glimmer of success, and because I enjoy the Brunetti family and the Venetian setting.  But every time, I watch Brunetti running up against corruption and/or incompetence, and walking away defeated.  The only case I can recall having a sort of fitting ending is the one where a bereft mother takes the law into her own hands.  If I take the books as an accurate depiction of Italy, it makes the country seem worse than Martin Cruz Smith’s Russia, pre- or post-Soviet era.  I’m left with two questions: Why would Brunetti keep fighting on when he loses almost every time, if not every time, and why does Leon want to write about a country she seems to loathe so much, and won’t even let her books be translated in Italian because she knows how they will be received, but keeps writing them?  Is she working out her own vendetta against Italy

Overall the book is enjoyable, the writing is colorful and interesting, even for a history book. But I started to question facts, "how would she come to that conclusion?" In full disclosure, I am not inclined to research documents I don't possess, and don't have the time to verify everything, but when I came to page 120, citation 32, I was pretty sure she had biases that were guiding her writing rather than facts. She wrote that George Washington's dentures were made of the teeth of his slaves conjuring up visions of him going out to their quarters with a pair of pliers and yanking out the teeth. In fact, according to research that I did perform, poor people and slaves did sell their teeth for money for food or whatever they needed money for. Her depiction of "dentures made from ivory and from nine teeth pulled from the mouths of his slaves" is highly tainted and offensive to me. I intend to keep reading but I must admit I have serious doubts about whether I will take her seriously after this. I could get this kind of propaganda from a Michael Moore video, if I wanted to.

I had a copy of this book in my classroom resources, and I removed it immediately. The time of talking about buying pets in pet stores is over. It has been proven time and time again that pet store dogs are from puppy mills. If you're not familiar with puppy mills, then a quick internet search will provide the details. The diseases, genetic disorders, malnutrition, broken and misshapen bones from the cages, females being bred literally to death, lack of sanitation, etc. Many states, counties, and cities across the country now ban pet stores that sell dogs and/or have laws against puppy mills and overbreeders. Don't promote shopping for dogs--the money they take keeps puppy mills in business. Before You Were Mine by Maribeth Boelts,  Maverick and Me by Katherine Schwarzenegger, and Buddy Unchained by Daisy Bix are good alternatives. If you have your heart set on singing a song, then look up the remakes of How much Is That Doggie in the Window by the Humane Society and by Doris Day. "Adopt, don't shop" is an important message, and my students aren't too young to learn about its importance.

I do not say this lightly, but I really didn't want this book to end, so much so, that I reached out to the author, fyi, she has a Social Media account, just to ask her if there would be a second book because I didn't want to leave this world, Professors Wilde and Bambleby and the Hidden Folk. Her answer was 'yes!'

Professor Emily Wilde is persistent, she has studied the faire folk all of her professional career and a trip to the remote and tiny village of Hrafnsvik to track down the most elusive of fae, the Hidden Ones, is just what she needs to truly distinguish herself in the world of Fairy Academia.

Her determinations is there but her skills at living in an icy village is what kept me reading through the first chapters. Emily finds connecting with people difficult. She doesn't manage to endear herself in her first days, in fact, she offends several people that could be absoultely vital to her research and this is when her rival, Professor Wendell Bambleby arrives.

The interactions between Wendell and Emily are hysterical at times, he's so affable and unaware, her irritated and snappy replies were so lively I could mentally visualize them in a way that isn't always possible for me with books. I can't wait to hear this on audio, maybe with a waspy tongued narrator emoting all of Emily's annoyance at Wendell's many distractions.

But the main mystery is all about the Hidden Ones, with enough danger nipping at the edges of the village to make even a daring researcher like Professor Wilde pause, but with her curiosity and career ambitions on the line, she presses forward and this is when the story became even more interesting. Because for awhile, I thought that perhaps the stories Emily was there to investigate were just that, stories.

A tiny warning, after the finding of the tree, without telling you what happens, there are some truly frightening bits that happen. I wasn't entirely sure what would happen to all the people I liked and it kept me awake worried for them. Again, I don't want to give anything away (actually, I do, I want to blab all of it, but I wont), except that the ending was quite unexpected and delightful and I really cannot wait to read book two.

***THIS REVIEW CONTAINS SPOILERS!!!***

This book had me waiting around for Ashton Kutcher to show up and tell me I was being punked. The plot itself is as old as time: someone with unique abilities is destined to save the world. But the execution was so incredibly haphazard, that was left with millions of questions that the editor should have asked before saying it was good to go.
I've listed some of them here, if you can answer them, please do!!
1. What was the point of having a spirit face if it was such an embarrassment to have someone see it? The book said it makes you stronger and more connected to your special abilities, so why would that make someone feel ashamed? Wouldn't you feel naked without it? Like an archer without his bow? Also, if it's so embarrassing, isn't it like an extreme form of exploitation to have the wrestlers show their spirit faces for entertainment? None if that made sense to me.

2. What was the point of masquerades? They seemed to be a somewhat restricted form of magic where you were able to summon a great being from beyond. Were the ones we encountered in the book just the worst ones or were there good ones too? Like masquerades that would come out of a termite mound and help you study for your math test. Were the summoners supposed to be able to control them? This was never explained in the book.

3. Why doesn't Sunny have any basic survival instincts? In order to become privy to something that she doesn't know anything about, she has to swap blood with one classmate and one stranger. She even mentions the fear of AIDS but does it anyway! Why?? Even if she was beyond curious (and it didn't really read like that in the book), shouldn't she have insisted more on a more health-conscious option? Fine, she does it and I guess doesn't get HIV. Now she has to cross a bridge using a power she just learned or she'll get eaten by a river monster?? Fine she makes it, now go through this dangerous forest where people get killed all the time. She barely survives... sure. Now she's spending afternoons with older men that she doesn't know and her parents don't know where she is. Sunny!! Wake up, girl! These are not smart choices! You are going to get snatched or killed! Not at one point in the book is she thrust into unavoidable danger. They give her a choice, and despite the fact that she doesn't know ANYTHING, she does it anyway. Why?

4. The money! So they keep saying that the only way to get it is by gaining knowledge, but then you can spend it!! Then can't you also get it by providing goods and services like every other monetary society?? So when you give merchants the money does it just disintegrate? And if so, what incentive is there to have a shop? The idea sounds nice, money for knowledge. But without envisioning a new system in which that makes sense, it don't work. Also, in the end, they killed people and got money. Are sunny and the gang now professional assassins? Guess it's good for kids to know all their career options!!!

5. What is the age range supposed to be for this book? One minute I'm reading about two men fighting to the death for sport, the next I'm reading 10 pages about a soccer game. One minute I'm reading about an adorable little bug that turns rubbish into art, and the next I'm reading about kids getting their eyes gouged out by a serial killer. The book has no cohesion in that sense (or any sense).

6. What was the point of Sunny having a foot in both worlds as the author put it? She never uses this skill the whole book. She doesn't even try to use it. They bring it up multiple times, but it has no bearing on the plot at all. And they said there were leopard people all over the world, so I assume some of them are white. They have white skin, does that make them ghost-like and thus connected to the spirit world?

7. Why was it specifically mentioned that the Black Hat was going to mix the poison he was giving to the sacrifices with Fanta? Why?

8. Why was nothing adequately described?? Most of this book was dialogue, and boring dialogue at that. This is a fantasy novel. Many more of it's pages should have been dedicated to describing this new world. Saying someone had "black, black, black" skin is laaaaaazyyyyyy!!!!!!!

9. Why is every single character sassy and hot-tempered? Thay are all so quick to fight either verbally or physically. It was exhausting to read. I wanted them to grow up, learn to work together, trust each other. In the end, they all just did their own thing against the bad guy until they were incapacitated, and then Sunny INEXPLICABLY does some juju that saves everyone.

10. Why were all the adults absolutely worthless? Sunny's parents' only response to her breaking the rules is beating her. She didn't appear to be a disobedient kid before. Why didn't either if them ask her if something was wrong? All the teachers basically tell them to do life-threatening tasks to see if they're worth anything, and if they die, whateves, life be like that and you don't matter. Wow. Except for when we've run out of covens to send to their slaughter against Black Hat. Thanks. And even when they weren't sending them to their deaths, the teachers really didn't have much to offer them except constantly reminding them that life would go on without them.

11. How is it acceptable to just brush off the fact that they NEVER RECEIVED AN EXPLANATION FOR WHY THEY, INSTEAD OF THE EXPERTS, HAD TO FIGHT BLACK HAT???? The freaking kids even asked! How many kids did they send to their deaths?? Why couldn't they have done it??

12. Why weren't their more examples of how magic is used? I felt like I didn't get a strong idea of how magic is a part of leopard culture. How have they used it over the centuries to shape their society? Why aren't there any formal magical schools for new learners? I assume there are more laymen than masters, why is there this weird mentorship program? How is magic used in daily life for people that don't want to be masters? I also wanted more information about how one could move in and out of leopard and lamb society. It seemed rather fluid, but I wanted more information.

13. Why didn't we meet any other magical students? I felt like I couldn't get a good grasp on how these kids were developing as compared to their peers. How did their lives differ? Were Sunny and the gang having a harder or easier time learning? Were any of them prodigies?

14. When Chichi didn't want to reveal her age I was like, well this is a pretty boring thing to make a mystery in this book. And then she and Sasha start dating and it's like, okay. Funs over. How freaking old are? State your age or step away from the minor.

15. I didn't feel like the author did a good job describing Nigerian culture. I felt like I was getting the Wikipedia version of what the country is like. It read like the author had never lived there for long and didn't really emerse herself in the cultures there. I especially felt that she did a poor job depicting African-Americans. Either get into the racial complexity of American culture or don't, but having one of the few African-American characters shout, you have no idea what it's like to be a black man in America and then talk about how he wishes the buffet had fried chicken and collard greens made me feel like she watched Friday, and was like, yeah, I get black people now. I know none of that was a question, but it had to be said.

16. Last thing, at one point, the author calls the actions of the Black Hat, "debauchery." Throwing eggs at a house is debauchery. Switching the salt and the sugar is debauchery. Skipping class is debauchery. Murdering and/or mutilating children is not debauchery.

Anyway, overall, bad book. Poorly written, full of holes, unbelievable and unlikable characters, and no cohesion. The story read to me like the author put a whole bunch if cool ideas into a hat, put them randomly into an empty journal, and then tried to connect them with loose dialogue and transitions. Just because it seems cool, doesn't mean it works!! Sometimes you have to let go of an idea you really like for the sake of the general readability of the novel.

At thirteen, Ruthy Ramirez disappeared sometime after track practice. We never meet her father. He died a few years after Ruthy disappeared. Dolores, her mother, went a bit mad. It is 2008. Nina just graduated from her premed program at an elite school. She avoided going home for college breaks and has not seen her oldest sister Jessica or her mother, Delores, for two years. Now, twelve years after Ruthy disappeared, Nina's coming back to Staten Island. Jessica has a baby and a full time job. It's time Nina helps take care of Dolores. After Ruthy did not come home, Dolores gave up her Catholic faith, opting to go to a Pentecostal Church with her dear friend Irene. She is teaching a parenting class at the church for women referred by the child services agency. And always present for them is Ruthy's absence.

So, there is a pervasive overlay of sadness throughout this story. Of course there is. But Jimenez captures so well the day to day lives of a close knit family that squabbles and juggles child care, pours love into cooking and cleaning, and working. The young women are smart and have dreams that you know are achievable. Nina didn't get into medical school. Jessica didn't finish college. But you know they won't stay in the low level jobs they work to make ends meet.

We smile -- a lot-- at the alternating narratives of these women, their thoughts about each other, about their bosses and coworkers, about Jessica's boyfriend, about their shared history that is more than but always includes the day Ruthy disappeared. We feel warmly toward them. We root for them. And we root for Ruthy. Because here and there, Ruthy tells the story of that day, filled in as well by Nina's and Jessica's observations. Her family acknowledges to us, what they did not tell the police: It is very possible Ruthy ran away that day. She was kind of wild. She once disappeared overnight. And that possibility leads to a whole chain of events that advance publicity on this novel spilled far too much. Just in case you have not read the advance publicity, I am not going to talk about it. It makes for a great road trip story, followed by a hysterical and indescribable, yet perfectly described scene in a Boston club.

It's early times in 2023, but I think this will be one of my top books for the year. As I noted, Jiminez captures what it means to be family in all of its craziness and love and despair and resentment. In this case, the family is Puerto Rican and the different experiences of the first and second generation New Yorkers, steadily trying to move up and questioning how far they have made it is a central theme. It matters that Ruthy is Latina, a person of color and that her disappearance did not get any serious attention from the police. And that is a major, major part of the point. Yet every character is relatable, faults and all. Sisters have the same fights everywhere. Mothers have some method of bringing them together or of losing it with their children. This is undeniably a beautifully written Puerto Rican version of all this, but every reader will find it familiar, while appreciating the culture and community of this particular family. I cannot recommend this book highly enough.

This book really missed the mark for me and I came away with the impression that the author was willing to sacrifice everything at the altar of getting to discuss pedantic detail about Mars. Initially, I didn't find this off-putting, but the further along the story crept, the more this became an unattractive quality of the book.

An illustrative example comes in the first quarter of the book wherein the difficulty of initially colonizing Mars is dismissed as easily as if it were a weekend glamping trip. Even as the author describes the exertion and exhaustion of the crew during the months following the landing, it felt like the hardship and sheer monumental difficulty of the task was given superficial treatment in favor of describing someone's toolbag by literally listing the 50 items inside or dedicating pages to the quality of Martian fines. I appreciate the research that went into these portions, but they do sometimes diverge into speculation that I don't find particularly interesting; particularly 30 years post-publishing.

Going beyond the descriptive nature of events to the characters themselves, I don't feel that the author successfully captured the emotional state of colonizing Mars. Neither through dialogue, developing characters' mental states (lookin at you robotic characters during the initial landing), nor through the nitty gritty of each page's focus did I feel that I was accompanying a character facing the terror, anxiety, excitement, tragedy of defeat, thrill of victory, etc associated with colonizing mankind's second planet. The discursive nature of the author's preference for technical topics means character development and storytelling take a 3rd row back seat. This left the whole work unappetizing, less like a narrative that could have explored these concepts in tandem with evolving events and more like a trade periodical that I skip around.

I found it emblematic of the entire work that during the colonization effort the author repeatedly TOLD me how characters were constantly engrossed in conversation and outwardly apparent emotional states, but chose to always move on from those moments in short order. It would've been a stronger work had the author taken a few pages to explore those things rather than quickly telling me they exist. But, we gotta get back to those tools and those fines, they aren't going to catalog themselves

A true "guided journal" for kids that focuses on exploration and observation is a tremendous tool to get kids outside and exploring. While this book shares that description, it doesn't execute.

The book starts out with some explanations for each chapter that give some background knowledge on each area of exploration - air, water, soil/rocks, plants and animals - and then gives children a hypothetical question that will require a lot of internet research to complete.

There are a few good prompts that will involve them actually going outside and looking at things, but the vast majority of them offer questions that deal with far away places or hypothetical questions that you need to delve into National Geographic for. There are very few "find this and look at it" style questions, which is kind of the point of the whole "spark adventure" and "explore" piece in the first place.

We're keeping this book to teach our daughter how to do research on the internet. So for it's purpose, it's a solid fail, but there is some value in having some intriguing questions to research...we'll just do it indoors.

Reason has brought us further than all the ravings of the past, which really has been mostly nightmare—'reason and the ability to dispassionately observe the koïnos kosmos, common reality' rather I should say.

Mr Jodorowsky may beg to differ,, but note that in his little fable he feels the need 0.) to construct straw-men of reason to mock, and 1.) to back its moral with observable outcomes (spoilers!)—prophetic visions all come true, an improbable bet is won, an old man is made physically young, a woman becomes androgynous through will alone, a dead person is resurrected, ten times over people who ought to've died miraculously are saved—that are not consonant with reality as it is. It's fine to say that it were preferable that things be as they are in this book, but they are not, and—much as "Stranger in a Strange Land"'s and "Atlas Shrugged"'s and "Victoria"'s and philosophies are 'validated' by the 'events' that 'take place' in their books—beliefs are not proofed by fictional events written by people creating them precisely to make us believe that things are so.

It would take a lot to make me dislike Moebius' art, though, and if you're good at disbelieving non-arguments, I can recommend the book.

This book started with an intriguing premise – Groundhog Day meets Agatha Christie. The protagonist has to find a killer by reliving the day of a murder eight times in the persona of eight different people who are all attending an English house party weekend. However, it soon became apparent that there was no way a reader can follow the plot and try to solve the mystery, because there is no bedrock of true facts in the book. Because of the set-up of the plot, which is quite convoluted, there is no way to know if anything that is said or done is true. Imagine trying to read a mystery novel where all the facts and clues are held up and reflected in a hall of broken mirrors, and you’re pretty close to the experience of reading The 7 ½ Deaths of Evelyn Hardcastle. In the end, which for me was about halfway through the book, I realized I was reading words, but those words had no discernible foundation of a story to justify my continued reading.

Having read all of the Richard Jury series over the years, I was frequently still left confused by The Old Success.

The introductory crime is fine, but from there on in it seems like the rest of the novel is an outline of a future book, rather than a fully developed book. Characters are introduced or called back from earlier novels at a breakneck speed with little explanation. Much of the plot depends on you recalling details from earlier Richard Jury mysteries, with no re-hashing or plot summaries provided in-world.

Compared to The Knowledge, from the year before, The Old Success is a much shorter, sloppier and more confusing novel. It could have benefitted from expansion, development and edits.

The Old Success is by far the worst Richard Jury mystery to date.

Risk was amazing! The second book in the Gentry Brothers series and it was another winner! Creed Gentry may be rough around the edges and one look from him would probably make you wet your pants but kindness wasn't something he and his brothers (they are triplets) were used to. They grew up poor and abused and they had to learn to be hard because love wasn't something they knew. They weren't looking for love. They were just living as best they could and they stay together no matter what because together they are safe. They take care of each other. In Book 1 Draw we saw Cord and Saylor fall in love despite a rough start. But they got past it and helped to heal one another. Moving on to book 2. Risk. Creed and Truly. Truly is Saylors bestie and she had no interest in being another notch on Creed Gentrys bed post. Until she did. Truly had her own secrets and history. It ate at her on a regular basis. She's a beautiful person inside and out. Yet, her life wasn't all sunshine and fun. She had a not so good life herself. They came together and both thinking that's it, that one time and walk away. But something happened to both of them and once was never gonna be enough. I love when a story has a unlikely couple get together and they unknowingly start to heal each other. There are moments that will make your heart hurt for them both. And moments that have more than your heart melting and sighing. I don't want to give too much away but really this story shows how it doesn't matter where you came or who, only you can change your future. You and you alone can chose to be different. To take a different road so to speak. And love, real, true and unrequited love can really change your life. These boys have found that in their women who have also not had the best life but chose to change their futures. Truly and Creed needed each other. And it was beautiful when they both realized it. If I wasn't so tired I'm sure I'd word this all better but all I can really day is read these books. They give you everything. There is lessons to be found and learned in these pages and hope. I loved both books. Their stories will stay with you. I love books that make you really look at your own life and think wow am I lucky. Maybe things weren't storybook perfect but what those boys went through I don't know how they survived it. My heart hurt for those little boys. And the mama in me was very angry at theirs for not protecting them. I couldn't imagine no matter how scared I was not protecting my babies. But those boys had to learn how to survive every day and take care of each other. I know they are just characters but I'm so proud of them. To Author Cora Brent, tha k you for giving us The Gentry Boys. For writing their stories and making us readers think and feel to the point we could see the dirt and feel their pain, their brotherly love and then letting us see them fall in love and start to heal. I cant wait to dive into the next book and learn more about their lives. Thank you ❤️

I always check the zippers on kids' clothing, and this one did not disappoint.  It is very high quality and easy to move up and down.  In case your child does not want to zip the jacket, there are snaps that he can use instead.  There are three little pocket zippers, and these are not quite as easy to pull up and down, but they are okay, and they did not dissuade me from recommending this jacket.  I like the fact that there are pockets, as many kids' jackets do not have them. The hood is fine, and it is detachable if your child does not like it for some reason. Though the price is a little high, the durability of the jacket makes it worth the investment. And it is machine washable!  Highly recommended.
